executive_summary: USD/CAD closed at 1.3968 on 30 October 2026, which means the Canadian dollar strengthened 1.79% over one month and 0.66% over three months, weakened 2.22% over six months and is 0.21% stronger over twelve months; the pair has retreated from its 52-week high of 1.43015 on 9 October and traded at 1.3969 intraday on 23 October, the strongest CAD level since 16 September [7]. The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate 25bp to 2.50% on 28 October, its first hike since July 2023, and its October Monetary Policy Report lifted the end-2026 inflation projection to about 3.4-3.5% from 2.4% while keeping inflation at or above 3% through much of 2027 [1][2][3]. Markets then priced a 45% chance of a December move and a second hike fully by January, while the domestic data turned against the Bank: August GDP was flat, September is estimated at -0.1%, third-quarter growth is tracking 1.3% annualised against the Bank's 2.0%, and employment fell 68,300 in September with unemployment at 6.5% [4][5][13]. Core inflation does not support a tightening cycle: CPI-trim is 1.8% and CPI-median 1.9%, so the 3.1% headline is an energy story, with gasoline up 27.8% year on year [10]. Valuation is cheap: the BIS real effective exchange rate of 95.59 for September is the lowest reading since at least January 2024, and CAD is 16.5% below its World Bank PPP value against the US dollar (PPP-implied USD/CAD 1.1667, best available, flagged as of 2026-10-31) [35][36]. The key tension is a terms-of-trade windfall from NYMEX WTI near USD 102, a second-quarter current account surplus of C$8.84bn and a short-CAD speculative base of 96,747 contracts, against a Bank that is hiking into stagnation, a 50% US tariff on C$20bn of exports and a WCS discount of USD 27 that caps how much of the oil price Canada keeps [11][25][27]. We are Neutral tactically (score +0.0139, conviction 2) and Bearish strategically (score -0.1219, conviction 2): the hike and the oil rally are in the price at 1.3968, and we expect USD/CAD to hold 1.39-1.41 into the December meeting before drifting toward 1.4150 by April 2027 as the market prices the shortest Canadian tightening cycle in 30 years against a Fed that is not easing [6].

valuation.trade_weighted_assessment: With roughly 70% of goods exports going to the United States (the non-US share was 30.2% in August), USD/CAD is the trade-weighted exchange rate in all but name [14]. CAD is 16.5% cheap to the US dollar at PPP and also cheap to GBP, CHF, AUD, NOK and SEK, though expensive against EUR, JPY, NZD and SGD, while its real effective rate fell over a year in which Canadian headline inflation ran near 3%, a real depreciation that is already offsetting part of the 50% tariff on C$20bn of exports [25].
valuation.what_is_priced_in: At 95.59 the REER prices a persistent tariff discount on Canadian exports and a policy rate that stays 125-150bp below the Fed. It does not price a successful steel and auto tariff agreement, which officials on both sides described as under negotiation on 26-27 October [26]. The valuation therefore embeds a one-sided trade-policy risk premium that a deal would release.
valuation.actionability: Structural, not tactical: a 16.5% PPP gap to the US dollar has persisted for years and has no mean-reversion clock inside four weeks. It becomes actionable only alongside a catalyst that removes the tariff discount, such as an agreement before the threatened 50% steel and auto tariffs of 1 January 2027 [26].

tactical.analysis: The Bank of Canada raised the overnight rate target 25bp to 2.50% on 28 October, its first hike since July 2023, leaving it 6th of the ten G10 policy rates, level with the ECB deposit rate, 137.5bp below the Fed funds midpoint of 3.875% and 210bp below the RBA's 4.60% [1][32]. The decision was almost fully priced: interest-rate futures had moved from about 30% to roughly three in four by the time of the Reuters poll published on 23 October [6] and about 80% on 23 October [7], and that poll had 19 of 34 economists calling it [6]. After the decision markets priced a 45% chance of a second hike on 9 December and a second hike fully by January, and after the flat August GDP print on 30 October they shifted to a December hold with 25bp to 2.75% in January [4][5]. We agree with the December hold, which we put at 65%, but we assign only 55% to a January hike, so the market's roughly 25bp for January is about 11bp too high on our numbers. The 2-year Government of Canada yield at 3.31% is 81bp above the policy rate and 130bp below the US 2-year at 4.61%, so the front end already discounts two to three further hikes over two years [18]. Against the US, the policy gap narrowed from 162.5bp to 137.5bp with the hike, but two FOMC dissents for a hike on 28 October mean the next move in the gap is as likely to widen it again as narrow it [32]. Carry is negative against the US dollar, sterling, the Australian dollar and the krone, and only CAD/CHF and CAD/JPY earn meaningful positive carry, so the rate channel gives CAD no tactical tailwind beyond what the hike delivered. The forces are offsetting: a hawkish Bank that has just tightened against an over-priced January path and a Fed that is closer to hiking than easing, which is a Neutral at moderate confidence.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices a December hold and a full 25bp hike by January, taking the rate to 2.75%; we price 35% for December and 55% for January, about 11bp less tightening by end-January. strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the question is how far the Bank of Canada can tighten into an economy that grew an estimated 1.3% annualised in the third quarter against its own 2.0% projection, and our answer is one more hike at most [5][15]. The Reuters poll median has the rate peaking at 2.75% after one more hike before end-March, what the poll describes as the shortest tightening campaign in 30 years, and the Bank's own neutral range of 2.25-3.25% means even 2.75% is barely restrictive [3][6]. Core inflation is the binding constraint on the hawks: CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9% are both below the 2% target, so the case for hikes rests on a headline driven by gasoline at +27.8% year on year [10]. Peers are moving the other way: the BoE is expected to hike to 4.00% on 5 November, the RBA to 4.85% on 3 November, the RBNZ to 3.00% on 9 December and the BoJ to 1.50% by January, so CAD stays 6th of ten, tied with the ECB, but its gap to the five higher-yielders widens by 25-50bp each even if the Bank hikes once more [40]. Against the US the gap stays wide: we expect the Fed at 3.75-4.25% and the Bank at 2.50-2.75% through April 2027, a 112.5-162.5bp differential that keeps carry against CAD at 1.1-1.6% a year. Six-month forward carry therefore narrows against JPY and widens against GBP, AUD and NZD, a net deterioration for CAD in the G10 carry ranking. The bull case, a Bank that hikes twice to 3.00% as inflation expectations rise toward the 3.7% one-year business reading, requires core inflation to turn, which the 0.18% monthly trim and median prints (about 2.2% annualised) do not yet show [10][23]. On balance the relative rate path is a moderate CAD negative over the strategic horizon.

tactical.analysis: Headline CPI rose to 3.1% year on year in September from 3.0%, below the 3.2% consensus, with a 0.1% monthly rise against 0.2% expected [10]. The Bank of Canada's preferred core measures are below target and falling: CPI-trim slipped to 1.8% from 1.9% and CPI-median to 1.9% from 2.0%, an average of 1.85%, while CPI-common fell to 2.4% and the Bank's ex-eight-volatile-components measure to 2.2% [10]. The gap between headline and core is almost entirely energy, with energy prices +19.0% and gasoline +27.8% year on year, so the inflation is cost-push with limited second-round evidence so far; food from stores at +1.7% is the lowest since May 2024 [10]. Activity has stalled: August GDP was flat against a +0.2% consensus, the September advance estimate is -0.1%, and third-quarter growth is tracking about 1.3% annualised against the Bank's 2.0% October projection [5][15]. The labour market is weakening: employment fell 68,300 in September after about 42,000 in August, unemployment rose to 6.5%, participation fell to 64.8% and average hourly wages rose only 2.3% year on year [13]. Leading indicators are mixed to soft, with the Ivey PMI at 58.2 against a 65.2 forecast, the S&P Global services PMI at 48.3 and the manufacturing PMI at 51.5, while August retail sales rose 1.2% and September's flash estimate is +0.7% [7]. The data flow has surprised to the downside on every major release in October except retail sales and the trade balance, so the surprise momentum is negative. For the 6 November employment report we expect a third consecutive decline of about 15,000 and unemployment at 6.6%, against a market that is pricing a January hike on the assumption that the labour market stabilises.

strategic.analysis: Over six months Canada's growth gap with the United States is the main channel from this factor to the currency, and it is widening: the OECD's quarterly national accounts, in its vintage of 31 October 2026, put US GDP growth at 2.07% year on year in the third quarter against 0.95% for Canada. The Bank's October projections assume growth of 2.0% in 2027, and the Reuters poll median is 1.7%, with fourth-quarter growth forecast at 0.8-1.3% annualised as the August tariff escalation feeds through [2][6]. Housing, the most rate-sensitive sector, is already contracting, with CREA reporting September sales down 7.7% year on year, prices down 1.6% to $666,538, and a third downgrade of its 2026 sales forecast to -5.2% [24]. The inflation trajectory depends on oil rather than domestic demand: the Bank projects headline at about 3.4-3.5% by year-end and at or above 3% through much of 2027, while core measures run at 1.8-1.9% [2][3]. Business inflation expectations are the hawkish risk, with one-year expectations at 3.7% and two-year at 3.1% in the third-quarter Business Outlook Survey and half of firms planning to pass through costs [23]. If oil stays above USD 100, headline inflation near 3.5% and rising expectations could push core up to about 2.3% by the first quarter of 2027, which would justify the market's second hike. Our base case is that weak demand dominates: unemployment drifts to 6.7-6.8% by the first quarter of 2027, wage growth stays near 2-2.5% and core inflation holds below 2.2%. That combination is CAD-negative because it limits the Bank to one more hike while it leaves the US growth premium intact.

tactical.analysis: The VIX was 17.2 on 29 October, the 52nd percentile of its one-year range of 13.47-31.05 and up 1.16 points over a month, a mid-range reading that is neither risk-on nor stressed. Credit is the weaker signal: the US investment-grade option-adjusted spread of 89bp is at the 96th percentile of its one-year range and high yield at 326bp is at the 95th percentile, both wider over the month, which says credit markets are pricing more risk than equities. Equities are at records, with the S&P 500 having closed at a record 7,819 on 6 October, while Canada's TSX composite fell 1.74% to 35,620.03 on 30 October but is still up 1.32% over a month and 17.71% over a year [21][22]. CAD is a mildly risk-positive currency, and its sensitivity is lower than AUD's or NZD's because the US linkage anchors it; in the October rally CAD outperformed AUD and NZD (AUD/CAD -0.35%, NZD/CAD -1.34%) while the VIX rose. The oil channel is supply-driven, with Hormuz shipping attacks and the US-Israeli war with Iran keeping Brent futures near USD 110-114, so oil is rising on supply rather than risk appetite and is not a clean risk signal [29]. The regime is transitioning from risk-on equities toward a wider-spread environment, with credit spreads near one-year wides even as equity indices sit at records. The two tail risks that matter for CAD in four weeks are a credit-led risk-off, which would lift USD/CAD 1-2% as the US dollar outperforms, and a Hormuz de-escalation that cuts oil by USD 15-20, which would hurt CAD through terms of trade. Neither is our base case, and the current environment neither helps nor hurts CAD on a net basis.

Oil's supply-driven rally has a defined end-point in any Iran settlement, and a USD 20 fall in WTI would cost CAD roughly 1-1.5% against the US dollar on the historical oil sensitivity. tactical.analysis: Oil is the dominant input to Canada's terms of trade, and NYMEX WTI rose 14.1% in October to USD 102.00 on 29 October from USD 89.38 on 29 September, the 91st percentile of its one-year futures range [29]. The rally is supply-driven, with October bringing the most attacks on Hormuz shipping since 2017 and Brent futures above USD 117 the week of 20 October, so it is a pure terms-of-trade gain for an exporter like Canada [29]. Canada keeps less of it than the headline suggests: the WCS discount at Hardisty widened to USD 27.00 under WTI for November delivery on 16 October, more than USD 15 wider than a year earlier, on Venezuelan barrels into the US Gulf Coast, refinery disruptions and tight pipeline space [27]. Even so, a USD 102 WTI with a USD 27 discount implies a realised heavy barrel of about USD 75, well above the year-earlier level. The external accounts already show it: the second-quarter current account, released on 27 August and the latest quarterly figure, swung to a C$8.84bn surplus, the first since 2022 and the largest since 2005, on a C$12.2bn goods surplus, and the August merchandise surplus rose to C$4.2bn against a C$1.5bn consensus [11][14]. August energy exports rose 4.7% and exports to the US 8.1%, lifting the surplus with the US to C$11.2bn, while the non-US share of exports fell to 30.2% from 33.9% [14]. The September trade release on 4 November should capture the first full month of oil above USD 90 and keep the surplus above C$3bn. This is the clearest tactical CAD positive in the dossier, held to 60 by the WCS discount and the tariff drag on non-energy exports.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the external balance is CAD's strongest structural support, and the terms-of-trade gain from oil is large enough to sustain a current account surplus of about 0.5-1.0% of GDP as long as WTI stays above USD 85 [11]. Canada is the world's fourth-largest crude producer, and 2026 output was expected in June to exceed 2025's record of 5.3mb/d, so volumes are rising into the price spike rather than falling [28]. Pipeline capacity caps the gain: Trans Mountain was apportioned for June 2026 (latest available report, 12 June), its 300,000 bpd of planned additions do not arrive before end-2028, and the WCS discount of USD 27 reflects that egress is full [27][28]. Trade policy is the main external risk: the US imposed a 50% tariff on C$20bn of Canadian goods from 22 August (report of 23 August, the latest on the measure), Canada matched it from 8 September, and the US declined on 1 July to renew CUSMA for a new 16-year term, putting the agreement into annual review [25]. Section 232 tariffs of up to 50% on steel and 25% on cars remain, and the US has floated raising steel and car tariffs to 50% from 1 January 2027, while both sides were reported on 26-27 October to be negotiating relief on steel and autos [26]. Capital inflows into Canadian bonds of C$80.8bn in the second quarter show the surplus is being complemented by portfolio inflows when yields rise [11]. Against a strong energy balance, the non-energy export base faces a structural tariff discount, so we hold Bullish at moderate confidence. The factor would turn Neutral if WTI fell below USD 85 or the January 2027 tariff escalation went ahead without a deal.

tactical.analysis: The 28 October communication was a hawkish shift: Governor Macklem said the Governing Council agreed that risks to inflation had increased and there was less scope for monetary accommodation, and that there could be a need to raise the policy rate further [2]. The Monetary Policy Report raised the end-2026 headline inflation projection to about 3.4-3.5% from 2.4% in July and keeps inflation at or above 3% through much of 2027, with a return close to 2% only by the middle of 2028 [1][2][3]. The Bank also raised its growth projections, to 1.0% in 2026 and 2.0% in both 2027 and 2028, which removes the growth argument for waiting [2]. The guidance is conditional, not explicit: future decisions are one meeting at a time and the Bank will proceed carefully given the uncertainties, which leaves room for a December pause [2]. Markets have bought the direction but not the urgency, pricing a December hold and a January hike after the weak GDP data, close to the Bank's own conditional language [5]. The Bank's credibility is strong but contested: KPMG, writing on 7 October, attributed about 40bp of the September-October rise in five-year yields to what it called an ill-timed hawkish tone on 2 September, and RMG disputed how inflation can average 3% when it is 3.1% today [3][22]. The next communication, the summary of deliberations in the week of 9 November, will show whether the decision had dissent and how strongly a second hike was discussed. Tactically the hawkish tilt is a modest CAD positive because it limits how far the market can price out January before the December meeting.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the question is whether the Bank's inflation-first framing survives a stagnating economy, and its track record suggests it does not hike far into weakness [2][6]. The Bank held at 2.25% from October 2025 to September 2026 and then hiked once, so its reaction function shows a high bar for tightening; the Reuters poll calls the expected two-hike cycle the shortest in 30 years [6]. Its projection of 2.0% growth in 2027 already looks optimistic against third-quarter tracking of 1.3% and a 0.8% fourth-quarter estimate within its own report [2][15]. If growth undershoots by 0.5pp, the Bank's own framework would argue for stopping at 2.50-2.75%, which is what the market prices. Credibility is supported by inflation expectations: business one-year expectations of 3.7% are above the 1-3% target range, which gives the Bank cover to hold a hawkish tone even while pausing [23]. Governor Macklem's comment that the Bank can look through an oil shock only until it spreads is the key conditional, and spread is not yet visible in trim and median at 1.8-1.9% [10]. The January Monetary Policy Report is the next forecast round and the likely venue for a recalibration toward a pause. Credible but conditional guidance that the market already prices gives no strategic directional signal, so the factor is Neutral.

tactical.analysis: Three dated events dominate the next four weeks: the US midterm elections on 3 November, the federal budget on 5 November and the October employment report on 6 November [30][31]. Trade policy is the largest geopolitical risk for CAD, and it is two-sided: the US imposed a 50% tariff on C$20bn of Canadian goods from 22 August after talks collapsed, Canada retaliated on 8 September, and on 26-27 October both sides were reported to be negotiating relief on steel and car tariffs [25][26]. Industry representatives expect any deal to be targeted rather than comprehensive, and the US position is reported to be moving closer to Canada's, with midterm pressure from border-state Republicans cited as a factor [26]. We put a targeted steel and auto agreement before year-end at 30%, which would lift CAD 1-1.5%, and a new escalation in the next four weeks at 15%. The Middle East supply shock is the second risk: Brent futures fell USD 1.93 on 27 October on Iran talks, and a settlement that removed the Hormuz premium would take USD 15-20 off oil and 1-1.5% off CAD [29]. The budget carries modest event risk because the deficit path is already known to be deeper than planned, at C$65.3bn for 2026-27 [30]. CME implied volatility of 4.443% one month out against 3.99% realised prices a modest event premium of 0.45 vols for this cluster. The upside and downside tails are roughly balanced over four weeks, so the factor is Neutral.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the trade calendar turns against CAD: the US has floated raising tariffs on Canadian steel and cars to 50% from 1 January 2027, and CUSMA is in annual review after the US declined to renew it on 1 July [25][26]. The August collapse showed that agreements can unravel at the last minute, with Prime Minister Carney calling the US changes unfair, uneconomic and a challenge to the reliability of any deal [25]. Our probabilities over six months are 35% for a targeted steel and auto deal, 40% for the status quo and 25% for escalation to 50% tariffs on steel and cars in January, a distribution with a heavier CAD-negative tail [26]. The Canada and Ontario C$9bn support package for steel and autos signals Ottawa is preparing for a prolonged dispute rather than an imminent deal [26]. The Middle East is the second strategic risk: a settlement with Iran would remove part of the oil windfall that is CAD's main support, and UBS expects Brent near USD 110 to year-end only if disruption continues [29]. Domestic political risk is low, with no federal election due before October 2029. A US dollar sell-off after the midterms is the main CAD-positive event risk, though it helps CAD less than higher-beta peers (BBH, 1 October) [37]. On balance the six-month event distribution tilts CAD-negative.

tactical.analysis: Finance Minister Champagne will table the 2026 federal budget on 5 November, and the Parliamentary Budget Officer warns that new spending has pushed deficits about C$3bn a year deeper than it projected in June [30]. The spring update put the 2026-27 deficit at C$65.3bn and 2027-28 at C$63.1bn, and the PBO projects more than C$63bn in 2030-31 against Ottawa's C$53bn [30]. Fitch affirmed Canada at AA+ with a stable outlook on 14 July, its latest review, projecting general government gross debt rising to 92.1% of GDP in 2026 from 89.7% and a general government deficit of 2.4% of GDP, close to the AA median [12]. S&P and DBRS rate Canada AAA with stable outlooks, and Moody's long-standing Aaa rating has not been reconfirmed at a public source this month (best available, flagged) [20]. Federal debt charges are projected to rise from C$55.6bn to C$76.1bn over five years, which is the sustainability metric to watch as yields rise [30]. Bond supply is being absorbed: foreign investors bought C$80.8bn of Canadian bonds in the second quarter, and KPMG describes federal fiscal policy as pretty reasonable [11][22]. No free source publishes Canadian sovereign CDS. A budget that confirms the known deficit path is neutral for CAD; only a deficit above C$75bn or a new fiscal anchor breach would make this factor material in four weeks.

strategic.analysis: Over six months fiscal risk rises at the margin but stays below the threshold that moves CAD [12][30]. The PBO projects that Ottawa will miss its declining deficit-to-GDP anchor and that the operating budget balance target will slip to 2028-29 from the government's 2027-28 [30]. General government debt of 92.1% of GDP is about double the AA median of 46.3%, which is why Fitch rates Canada a notch below S&P and DBRS [12][20]. Rising yields compound the cost: the five-year yield neared 4% in early October, about 100bp above a year earlier, so debt charges will run ahead of the C$55.6bn to C$76.1bn path projected in 2025 [22][30]. Against that, fiscal support for tariff-hit sectors, such as the C$9bn steel and auto package, cushions growth and partially offsets tariff drag [26]. Provincial finances diverge, with energy-producing provinces benefiting from USD 100 oil while Ontario and Quebec carry the tariff burden. tactical.rationale: At tactical weights Policy and Rates (0.24) and Inflation and Growth (0.18) dominate, and they point in different directions for different reasons: the policy factor is Neutral because the 28 October hike to 2.50% was priced, while the growth factor is Bearish because August GDP was flat, September is estimated at -0.1% and employment fell 68,300 [1][5][13]. The weighted score of +0.0139 is Neutral, and the near-zero result reflects genuine offsetting forces rather than an absence of signals. Oil is the main CAD support, with NYMEX WTI up 14.1% in October to USD 102.00 and the August trade surplus at C$4.2bn, and the Bank's hawkish guidance limits how far January pricing can fall before the December meeting [2][14][29]. Positioning adds a modest bullish asymmetry, with leveraged funds net short 96,747 contracts, close to the 2026 extreme [34]. These positives interact: the oil windfall is the reason the Bank can sound hawkish, and the hawkish tone is the reason the leveraged short has not been rewarded. They conflict with growth: a third consecutive employment decline on 6 November would remove part of the January hike that the market prices and push USD/CAD back toward the 50/100-day averages at 1.403-1.405. What is priced is a December hold, a January hike and oil near USD 100; we expect a December hold but put only 55% on January, about 11bp less than priced. The path of least resistance is a range of 1.3880-1.4100 with a slight bias higher toward 1.4000 into mid-November. The key dated catalysts are the US midterms on 3 November, the September trade data on 4 November, the federal budget on 5 November, the October employment report on 6 November and October CPI on 16 November [31]. Conviction is low because the main bearish driver, weak domestic data, competes with an oil price that is set by Middle East supply rather than by Canadian fundamentals. The view is not a coin flip because the growth data have a measurable downside bias against a market that priced a stable labour market. Actionability is limited: with one-month implied volatility at 4.443% and a 14-day ATR of 64 pips, a 30-pip expected drift does not justify a directional position, and range strategies are better suited. The trade we would take is tactical: fade USD/CAD rallies toward 1.4100 and dips toward 1.3880 until the 6 November report resolves the growth question. A decisive close outside 1.3880-1.4100 after that report would be the signal to upgrade conviction.

The rate argument is that the Bank of Canada is tightening into stagnation, with third-quarter growth tracking 1.3% against its 2.0% projection, core inflation at 1.8-1.9% and a Reuters-poll peak of 2.75%, while the BoE, RBA, RBNZ and BoJ are all expected to hike and the Fed has two dissents for a hike [5][6][32]. That correlation is why conviction is low despite a Bearish score. assumptions: The Bank of Canada policy rate is taken as 2.50% from the 28 October 2026 announcement; daily central-bank policy-rate series compiled by the BIS still showed 2.25% on 26 October because they lag by six to ten days.

Carry is the policy-rate differential, annualised, divided by 60-day realised volatility of each cross from daily weekday closes to 30 October 2026; Singapore has no policy rate, so no CAD/SGD carry figure is shown.

Forward points are derived from the 137.5bp policy differential plus about 1.8bp of implied cross-currency basis, inferred from the 164.3bp roll premium on CME Canadian dollar futures on 28 October; no free source publishes 3-month CAD/USD, EUR/USD or JPY/USD cross-currency basis.

The Government of Canada 2-year yield is taken as 3.31% (30 October 2026); one wire report on 30 October gave 2.618%, which is inconsistent with the 3.413% close two days earlier and is treated as a reporting error.
The implied-volatility percentile compares the 36.7-day CME at-the-money volatility with six months of 20-day realised volatility, because no free one-year implied-volatility history is available.

PPP fair values use World Bank 2025 PPP conversion factors (GDP, local currency per international dollar); the factor values could not be displayed at the World Bank indicator page as of 2026-10-31, so they are best available, flagged. Germany stands in for the euro area; the BIS broad real effective exchange-rate percentile is measured over the 33 monthly readings from January 2024.
CFTC percentiles are measured over the 25 weekly futures-only reports from May to October 2026, so they describe the 2026 cycle rather than a multi-year history.

Peer GDP, unemployment and current-account figures are the OECD's 2026-10-31 vintages; Canada's third-quarter GDP figure of 0.30% q/q is the industry-based estimate and will be superseded by the expenditure-based release on 30 November 2026.
Moody's Aaa rating for Canada was not reconfirmed at a public source as of 2026-10-31 and is shown as best available, flagged; Canadian sovereign CDS is not published freely.
The January 2027 Bank of Canada decision date is not yet in the published schedule and is shown as 2027-01-W4.

seasonality.pattern: The documented CAD patterns are the federal budget cycle and fourth-quarter energy hedging: Canadian producers typically extend forward hedges into year-end, which sells US dollars against CAD. Year-end US dollar funding demand and portfolio rebalancing also fall inside the strategic horizon.
seasonality.relevance_window: 5 November 2026 (budget) through mid-January 2027 for producer hedging and year-end funding
seasonality.historical_magnitude: Producer hedging and year-end effects are typically 50-100 pips on USD/CAD and tend to reverse in January; with WTI at USD 102 the incentive to hedge forward production is stronger than usual.
seasonality.current_alignment: Partly against the strategic Bearish view: producer hedging at USD 100 oil supports CAD into December, which is why we expect the rise toward 1.4150 to come mainly after the 1 January 2027 tariff deadline.

factors_changed.reason: The Bank of Canada hiked to 2.50% on 28 October, narrowing the CAD-USD policy gap from 162.5bp to 137.5bp, and the market now prices a second hike by January; the residual mispricing is about 11bp, too small to support a directional tactical call.
August GDP was flat against +0.2% expected, September is estimated at -0.1%, employment fell 68,300 and core inflation slipped to 1.8-1.9%.
WTI rose 14.1% in October to USD 102.00 and the August trade surplus reached C$4.2bn, building on the C$8.84bn second-quarter current account surplus.
The Bank delivered the hike its September tone implied and signalled further increases may be needed, so its guidance and the market path are now aligned.
Steel and auto tariff talks resumed in late October, balancing the escalation risk inside four weeks; the strategic Bearish view is retained because of the 1 January 2027 deadline.
Funding stayed orderly with SOFR at 3.94% and reserves near USD 2.96tn, and the implied CAD basis is near zero, so the factor no longer adds a CAD-specific negative.
